title: Input and truthiness
summary: Read from the user, convert, and decide what counts as true.

steps.title: input() always returns a str
body: `input()` reads one line from standard input, like `Console.ReadLine()`, without the trailing newline. It always returns a `str`, so convert it:
`int("abc")` raises `ValueError` (C#'s `FormatException`). `int(" 42 ")` is fine: it ignores surrounding spaces.
Several numbers on one line? Split first: `a, b = map(int, input().split())`.

steps.prompt: The user types `5`. What does `print(input() * 2)` print?
steps.explain: `input()` gives the string `"5"`, and `str * int` repeats the string. Convert with `int(...)` before doing arithmetic.

steps.title: Add two numbers
prompt: Read two whole numbers, **on one line**, separated by a space. Print their sum.
hints: `input().split()` gives a list of two strings.

steps.title: Truthiness
body: In C# an `if` needs a `bool`. In Python **any object** can be tested, and these count as false:
Everything else is true. So the Pythonic way to say "if the list is not empty" is:

steps.explain: The string `"0"` and the list `[0]` are not empty, so they are truthy. Only empty and zero values are falsy.

steps.title: and / or return a value
body: `and`, `or` and `not` are words, not `&&`, `||`, `!`. They short-circuit like C#, but `and` / `or` return **one of their operands**, not necessarily `True`/`False`:
name = input() or "stranger"   # default when the line is empty
print(3 and 7)     # 7   last value if all truthy
`x or default` is the everyday cousin of C#'s `x ?? default`, but beware: it also replaces `0` and `""`, not just `None`.

steps.explain: `or` returns the first truthy operand, or the last one if none is truthy (so `[]`). `and` returns the last operand when all are truthy.

steps.prompt: Print `Hello, stranger` when the line is empty, otherwise greet by name.

steps.title: Greeter with a default
prompt: Read a name and an age on two lines.
- If the name line is blank (or only spaces), use `friend`.
- If the age line is blank, print just `Hello, NAME!`.
- Otherwise print `Hello, NAME! Next year you will be N.`
solution: print(f"Hello, {name}! Next year you will be {int(age) + 1}.")

tests.name: name and age
tests.expect: Hello, Mia! Next year you will be 31.

tests.name: blank name
tests.expect: Hello, friend! Next year you will be 10.

hints: An empty string is falsy, so `if age:` tests whether one was typed.
